Public Comment: The public is encouraged to address City Council on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other matter
within its jurisdiction subject to the rules of decorum described in Section 2.08.020 of the Norwalk Municipal Code. If you wish to
address City Council, please complete a speaker card and hand the card to the Sergeant at Arms. City Council will hear public
comment on items listed on the agenda during discussion of the matter and prior to a vote and on matters not listed on the
agenda during the Oral Communications period.

Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or unless certain
emergency or special circumstances exist. The City Council may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for
consideration at a future City Council meeting.

Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the City Council: Comments should be limited to 3 minutes or less
and
directed to the City Council as a whole and not directed to individual Councilmembers.

Americans with Disabilities Act: In compliance with the ADA, if you need special assistance to participate in a City meeting or
other services offered by this City, please contact the City Clerk’s department, (562) 929-5720. Assisted listening devices are
available at this meeting. Ask the City Clerk if you desire to use this device. Upon request, the agenda and documents in the
agenda packet can be made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability. Notification of at least 48
hours prior to the meeting or time when services are needed will assist the City staff in assuring that reasonable arrangements
can be made to provide accessibility to the meeting or service.

Note: Any writings and/or documents provided to a majority of the City Council regarding any item on this agenda after it has
been posted will also be made available for public inspection. Writings and/or documents are available for inspection in the City
Clerk’s Department, during regular business hours, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday – Thursday and 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., every
other Friday; telephone (562) 929-5720. You may also contact the City Clerk via e-mail at recordsrequests@norwalkca.gov.

  REGULAR MEETING

Vice Mayor Perez called the meeting to order at 6:05 p.m. in the Council Chambers,
Norwalk City Hall, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Responding to roll call
were Councilmembers Ramirez, Rios, and Valencia, and Vice Mayor Perez. Mayor Ayala
was absent. Also present were Jesus M. Gomez, City Manager; Arnold M. Alvarez, City
Attorney; and Theresa Devoy, City Clerk.

The invocation was delivered by Dr. George Bojorquez, New Creation Church of Norwalk;
followed by the flag salute, led by Young Marine Corporal Aiden Vaca, Lance Corporal
Kenneth L. Worley Young Marines.

CLOSED SESSION REPORT

The City Attorney indicated there was no reportable action taken on the matters discussed
in closed session.

CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS

Councilmember Valencia reported on her attendance at the Norwalk Lions Club
Community and Norwalk’s Food Distribution. Councilmember Rios shared that it is World
Cancer Day and urged all to stay healthy and focus on preventative care. Councilmember
Ramirez encouraged all to report concerns throughout the community such as broken
sprinklers, graffiti, and illegal dumping. Vice Mayor Perez highlighted the City’s “Norwalk
Connect” Application used to streamline reporting concerns; shared that City newsletters
were distributed, highlighting the “Norwalk’s Future” bulletin; reported on her attendance
at the Los Angeles Regional Homelessness meeting and shared plans to focus on
Measure A Funds to address homelessness issues being distributed throughout
Los Angeles County; and was a guest speaker at the Professional Police Officers
Association Annual Retreat.

SPECIAL PRESENTATIONS

City Council recognized Angel Tree Project and Stuff-A-Bus Project Sponsors.

City Council recognized the Winners of the 2024/25 Beverage Container Recycling &
Litter Prevention Artwork Contest.

Background:

The City of Norwalk provides rental uniforms and cleaning services for uniforms for the
Transportation Department’s Equipment Maintenance Mechanic and Equipment Service
Helpers, as well as related items including entry mats, cleaning cloths, etc. Currently, Unifirst
Corporation (Unifirst) provides these services for both Transportation Department staff and
Public Services Maintenance Workers by means of a cooperative agreement. Unifirst’s current
service agreement expires on May 31, 2025. The Transportation Department is seeking to
execute their own service agreement for rental and cleaning of uniforms and other related
products with Cintas Corporation (Cintas) via cooperative agreement from the State of California,
Department of General Services (DGS) Procurement Division, Invitation for Bid (IFB) 524994.
DGS allows participating cities and various government agencies to enter into agreements as
members and take advantage of large quantity bids and Request for Proposals nationwide.

Cintas would provide Flame Resistant (FR) uniforms for the Equipment Maintenance staff along
with entry mats, cleaning cloths and related items. The National Fire Protection Association
(NFPA) as well as Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) requires that
employees wear FR protective apparel whenever there is a possibility of exposure to electric arc
flashes or blasts. The Transportation Department has nine Battery Electric Buses (BEBs);
therefore, Equipment Maintenance staff are required to transition to FR uniforms. Cintas
provided a quote for FR uniforms for $318.78. The contract with Cintas would end June 30, 2027,
with two optional one- year extensions.

Background:

Keeping the community informed is essential, especially in times of crisis when information
spreads rapidly. Since August 2020, The Merino Group (TMG) has provided the City with daily
media tracking, crisis management, and strategic messaging to ensure clear and effective public
communication.

Under this proposed agreement, TMG will offer specialized "crisis communications" services that
are activated during emergencies or unforeseen events. These services will focus on effectively
managing crises, particularly in relation to:

  •  Public Safety Initiatives: Maintaining critical contact databases, coordinating closely with
  the Public Safety Department, and enhancing emergency preparedness through targeted
  messaging and effective crisis response strategies.

  •  Community Improvement Projects: The communicating of City-led initiatives on housing
  density, parking solutions, and traffic mitigation to keep residents informed about new
  developments and their impact.

  •  Public Engagement: The implementation of outreach programs, including surveys and
  focus groups, to provide City officials with community-driven insights on public safety and
  municipal services.

  •  Litigation Communications: Development of a strategic messaging framework to align
  public communications with the City’s legal strategy regarding ongoing litigation with the
  state of California.

During a crisis, the priority is to provide urgent, accurate information to manage the narrative,
address public concerns, and connect residents to resources.

As a sole-source provider, TMG is uniquely positioned to offer crisis communications services,
demonstrating a deep understanding of the City's challenges and a proven history of
successfully managing city-led initiatives during past crises. Additionally, their ability to

TMG will also monitor, assess, and respond to crises related to homelessness, crime, and

support, and rapid message deployment on urgent city matters.

This contract runs through June 30, 2025, with an option for a one-year extension.

   Scope of Work: Strategic Communications & Crisis Management Services

The Merino Group (TMG) will be providing comprehensive media monitoring and crisis
communications services for the City of Norwalk. This will include daily monitoring of
traditional and social media, identifying emerging issues requiring response, and if
necessary, proactively correcting misinformation. Under the present scope of work, “Crisis
communications” is defined as specialized communications services activated during
emergencies or unforeseen events, focusing on managing crises while safeguarding
public safety.

The primary objective will be to deliver urgent, accurate, and clear information to control
the narrative, address public concerns, and if necessary, guide the residents of Norwalk to
essential resources. This service is distinct from general communications services, which
focus on regular updates on city services and events. TMG may work directly with our
general communications services in directing public information and using city
communication channels to ensure the accurate delivery of facts to prevent confusion and
ensure effective resolution of any crises.

Building on their monitoring services, TMG will provide strategic crisis management
support across high-priority areas including homelessness, crime prevention,
development projects, and environmental incidents. Their crisis response capabilities
include 24/7 media relations, Spanish-language communications expertise, and rapid
deployment of messaging across relevant channels. TMG may also prepare city leadership
for media interactions and provide real-time guidance during emerging situations that
impact community welfare.

This service may include:

Public Safety Initiatives

TMG will be maintaining critical contact databases, conducting targeted research, and
coordinating with the Public Safety Department to ensure consistent and effective
messaging to the community. These efforts enhance emergency preparedness, improve
crisis response strategies, and ensure that public safety communications remain clear,
timely, and aligned with community needs.

Community Improvement Projects

TMG will assist in the communication of the City’s planned execution of community
development initiatives. By analyzing data and collaborating with municipal departments,
TMG will help implement projects that address the challenges with housing density,
 limited parking, traffic mitigation to ensure the community is informed regarding the
City’s new development projects and its mitigation efforts on these projects.

Public Engagement Initiatives

To strengthen trust and transparency, TMG may implement as needed, community
outreach programs, including surveys and focus groups, that gather actionable insights
on policing programs and municipal services. These initiatives provide Ccity officials with
valuable feedback, enabling them to refine policies, improve service delivery, and address
public safety concerns.

Litigation Communication Services

As the City of Norwalk faces litigation from the state of California, a strategic and
disciplined communications approach may be essential to protect its reputation, inform
key stakeholders, and maintain public confidence. This scope outlines the key deliverables
and services required during the litigation process, ensuring messaging remains clear,
consistent, and aligned with the legal strategy.

TMG will develop a strategic messaging framework, crafting key narratives that articulate
the City’s position while mitigating potential legal risks. This may include talking points
for City officials, a messaging guide for public-facing statements, and a set of FAQs to
ensure internal consistency. Early coordination with legal counsel will align public
messaging with the city’s legal defense.

  •  A comprehensive media relations strategy may be implemented.
  •  Internal communications will be crucial to keep City employees, council members,
  and key stakeholders informed as a direct outreach to other stakeholders,
  including business leaders, community organizations, and advocacy groups.
  •  Digital media, social media oversight, and digital engagement may be used as part
  of strategy development.

Housing Element

As California enforces its Housing Element requirements, Norwalk residents must be
informed about how these mandates may impact the community.

To ensure a robust public information campaign, TMG may be tasked with the following:

  •  Delivering clear, accessible messaging across multiple media platforms.
  •  Informational materials to explain the Housing Element process, outline the City’s
  concerns, and emphasize the importance of responsible planning.
   •  Executing a strong media and public relations strategy under the direction of City
  administration.

The state’s housing development approach raises challenges about local control,
infrastructure capacity, and public safety. This public information campaign will ensure
that Norwalk’s position is accurately conveyed, empowering the community to stay
informed and engaged.

SUBJECT: AGREEMENT FOR HOUSING LIAISON FUNDING

Background:

The City has been committed to addressing homelessness by providing much-needed services
and housing navigation opportunities for the unsheltered population, as well as individuals from
throughout Los Angeles County (County) who come to Norwalk. To support this initiative, the
City sought Measure H funding from the County and the Gateway Cities Council of Governments
(COG) to aid in implementing the City's Homelessness Plan, which was updated in 2023. The
City’s Homelessness Plan identified the need for a Housing Liaison to help place this large influx
of unhoused residents into interim or permanent housing as expeditiously as possible.

To achieve this, the County agreed to provide funding for a Housing Liaison position, which will
be administered by COG. The Housing Liaison will be deployed in the field with the City’s HOPE
teams or, based on the City’s operational needs, help screen tenants and assist with their
placement. The role’s objective will be to help transition residents into housing within one year.
It is estimated that the Housing Liaison will be able to engage up to 100 persons, with at least
25 individuals being placed in interim housing and at least 25 individuals being placed in
permanent housing. They will also provide weekly reports to the City.

Fiscal Impact:

There is no fiscal impact to the City. The County will provide Measure H funding, administered
by the GOG, in an amount not to exceed $178,869 for the Housing Liaison position, activities
and use.

Services (2), and the Youth Commission (all 15). The Youth Commission does not have any

Two of the vacancies on the Art in Public Places Committee are appointed based on Norwalk
Municipal Code §15.44.060, and require consensus of the entire City Council. Any

Background:

Enclosed are mid-year budget projections for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2024/25 Budget. The
projections and recommended budget adjustments are based upon the final Audited Financial
Statements for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2024 and six months actual expenses and revenues
during the current fiscal year.

General Fund:

FY 2023/24

Based on audited results for fiscal year ending June 31, 2024, net of accounting Governmental
Accounting Standards Board (GASB) adjustments; overall revenues reached City’s estimates of
$77 million. However, the City’s Major Revenue category, which represents 83% of General Fund
total revenues and comprised of sales taxes, real property value derived revenues, other taxes and
franchise fees, underperformed the estimates by 1%, or $0.8 million. Departmental revenues made
up for the shortfall of Major Revenues and outperformed the budgetary amount by $0.9 million.
Expenditures were $6.9 million, 9% under the budget, due mainly to savings realized under:
Personnel ($4.4 million), Sheriff’s Contract ($1.1 million) and other expenditures ($1.4 million).

The outcome of the above mentioned financial impacts is the General Fund ending available
balance of $21.8 million, which is $0.8 million lower than anticipated during the preparation of the
FY 2024/25 Budget.

FY 2024/25

The current FY 2024/25 budget year-to-date results indicate that the City is on target with the
projections, except for the following:

Revenue Adjustments:

Even though, the overall General Fund revenues are expected to slightly outperform the original
budget estimates by a total of $0.8 million, or 1%, and reach $76.5 million, they are still lagging
behind the prior fiscal year revenues which were $77 million.

The proposed increase in General Fund revenues estimate encompasses a combination of the
following revisions:

Property value derived revenues represent the first most significant portion of General Fund
revenues. Projections for all categories combined are proposed to be increased by $624
thousand. The detail of adjustments is as follows:

  •  Property Tax In Lieu of VLF: This category is estimated to increase by 2% from the original
  FY 2024/25 projections. The City receives two equal allocations from the State in January
  and May. Based on the amount received in January, staff estimates this revenue will be
  $294 thousand higher than projected.

  •  Property Tax allocated to the City from Successors of the former Redevelopment Agencies
  is estimated to reach $1.3 million, which is $330 thousand higher than staff’s original
  estimates.

Sales Taxes – Local Tax & Measure P: The City’s second largest revenue category is $1.0 million
under the anticipated revenues and is expected to reach $25.1 million, representing a decrease
from the prior year’s actual revenue amount of $25.6 million. Some hardest hit categories affecting
the decline are general consumer goods and autos, resulting in sales tax not reaching the
projections. This negative adjustment reflects the state of the economy and is in line with regional
economy trends.

Utility User Tax (UUT): As the prices of electricity and gas continue to increase, so do the City’s
UUT revenues. Staff estimate this year the UUT will generate $5.8 million in revenues, $74
thousand over the original budget estimates.

Transient Occupancy Tax: Year-to-date receipts from local hotels are trending to reach $1.6 million,
which is $50 thousand lower than our original estimates.

Business License: The annual revenues are estimated to be $100 thousand under the budgeted
amount of $0.9 million.

Real Property Transfer Tax: Despite the decline in the number of single-family home sales, receipts
generated by real property sales transactions are outperforming projections by $13 thousand.
Revenues in this category remain steady primarily due to the continued increase in the average
and median sale prices of single-family homes in Norwalk.

Other General Fund revenues will increase by a net amount of $1.2 million, out of which $0.8 million
will be generated from Building & Safety plan check fees related to development projects. About
65% of these plan check fees collected will cover the increased cost of contractual plan check
services. Details of revenue budget revisions can be found in Exhibit A attached to Resolution No.
25-07.

Expenditure Adjustments:

The proposed mid-year budget revisions increase the operational spending by a net of $388
thousand. The most significant changes are as follows:

  •  Various personnel changes under full-time, part-time, overtime and related benefits will add
  about $331 thousand to additional personnel cost for the remainder of the fiscal year, which
  include:
  o City Clerk department will eliminate two full-time Office Assistant I positions, which
  became vacant due to the promotion to Office Assistant II positions.

  o Social Services department is requesting to add one new Social Services Worker II
  position to serve families in crises; two Community Workers will transfer from Social
  Services to the Public Safety department.

  o Engineering requests replacing the vacant Senior Management Analyst position with an
  Assistant Engineer position.

  o Various part-time hours and overtime wages adjustments are requested by Public
  Safety, Public Services, and Recreation departments.

  Additionally, long-term vacancies city-wide will reduce personnel cost by a net savings of $1.2
  million. The proposed personnel changes are detailed in Exhibit C to Resolution No. 25-07.

  •  Operations and maintenance budget requests resulting in a $1.4 million budget increase are
  requested to cover various departmental needs. Among the most significant requests are:
  $545 thousand for plan check services that are offset by increased revenues; $580 thousand
  to fund various contractual services city-wide; $42 thousand for computer software and
  support costs; and $104 thousand for various smaller expenses.

  •  To ensure compliance with the reserve policy, staff is proposing to increase the operating
  transfer in from the Highway User Tax Fund (HUT Fund). An additional $700 thousand
  transferred in from HUT Fund is essential to help offset street maintenance cost without
  compromising the City’s fund balance, for a total annual amount of $2.6 million.

  •  Additional appropriations to cover the capital outlays total $537 thousand and include two
  sets of meridian road barriers ($300 thousand) and funding for an electric batteries backup
  residential program ($200 thousand).

Proposed revisions to the General Fund expenditure budget are detailed in Exhibit B attached to
Resolution No. 25-07.

Taking into consideration the proposed budget revisions, the estimated unassigned General Fund
balance will be approximately $15.3 million, which is about $112 thousand over the City’s reserve
policy, currently set at 20% of operating and minor capital outlays budget. Exhibit D to Resolution
No. 25-07 provides more detail of the General Fund balance projections.

Special Revenue Funds:

Based on the actual results, staff also proposes various adjustments to expenditures and revenues
from Special Revenue Funds, identified in the Exhibit E attached to Resolution No. 25-07.

Significant budget revisions are proposed in the following funds:

Child Care: City will program additional $580 thousand in federal and state entitlement to provide
childcare services to qualified families.

Gateway Cities Council of Governments (GCCOG) - Measure H Pass-Through Grant: Effective
January 2025, the City entered into an agreement with GCCOG and secured funding not to exceed
$179 thousand, for a new Housing Liaison full-time position, which is proposed to be added to the
existing salary schedule.

COPS Grant: Overtime cost for the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s deputies is estimated to increase
by $150 thousand.

Equipment Replacement Fund: In addition to the GASB Statement 87 adjustment of $780,000 in
both revenues and expenditures, Public Safety is requesting $300 thousand to replace one
damaged camera trailer, and purchase two new ones to be used at the California Youth Authority
property and at newly remodeled parks.

Exhibit F attached to the Resolution No. 25-07 details proposed revisions to Various Capital
Improvement Projects funded from Special Revenue Funds:

Measure W Storm Water Grant: An additional $380 thousand will fund storm drain and catch basin
repairs citywide.

The City continues its commitment to rehabilitate local streets investing an additional $20 million
from available Special Revenue Funds, primarily from:

Road Maintenance Rehabilitation Fund: State funding earmarked for streets will provide $11 million
to pave local streets in Zones 2, 4, 7, 9, 29 and 31.

Street Renovation Fund: Staff are requesting an additional appropriation of $6.9 million from the
City’s capital reserves earmarked for streets to secure funding for pavement and traffic signal
projects in various zones city-wide.

Enterprise Funds:

Transportation: Staff is projecting an increase of approximately $1 million in operating revenues
and a $0.3 million net increase in operating expenses. Transportation budget revisions are
summarized in Exhibit G attached to Resolution No. 25-07.

Water: Revenue estimates can be increased by $140 thousand, and expenses are requested to
be increased by a net of $94 thousand. In addition, staff request funding ($200 thousand) for
Cerritos Water System Intertie Upgrade project.

Sewer: No significant budget revisions are requested.

The requested budget revisions for both Water and Sewer funds are detailed in Exhibit H attached
to Resolution No. 25-07.

Conclusion:

Staff is confident that the proposed mid-year revisions highlighted above and detailed in the
Exhibits attached to Resolution No. 25-07 are reasonable and within the guidance of preparing a
financial plan that will maintain required services within the City’s available resources. Personnel
changes affecting the Salary Schedule are reflected in Exhibit A attached to Resolution No. 25-08.

Fiscal Impact:

The requested mid-year adjustments to the General Fund estimated revenues total a net increase
of $830 thousand. The net increase in appropriations is $387 thousand. The Budgetary
Unassigned General Fund balance as of June 30, 2025, is expected to be $15.3 million absent any
future budget amendments approved by City Council.

The proposed revisions to the FY 2024/25 budget are subject to City Council review and
consideration and any approved modifications will be reflected in the balances of the appropriate
funds.
